title: Majestic Victory
summary: Walk away from the pawn to escape checks, then underpromote to a rook to avoid stalemate.

nodes.question: Can a lone pawn beat the rook?
nodes.explanation: The king’s square determines whether the rook can pin or skewer a promoted piece.

nodes.question: Where should the king go after the check?
nodes.explanation: One step can permit a pin; another can expose the promoted queen to a skewer.

nodes.question: Why would a rook be better than a queen?
nodes.explanation: Black has a rook sacrifice that draws against a queen but not against a rook.

branches.title: Walk the king down and choose a rook
commentary: White must turn the advanced pawn into a threat without allowing the rook to pin it or skewer the promoted piece.
c7 advances the pawn. The white king controls c6 and b7, while the pawn controls d8.
Rd6+ starts a series of checks. The rook wants the king to leave a square that protects the promotion plan.
Kb5 avoids the seventh-rank pin and keeps control of c6, where the rook would need to stand for a skewer.
Rd5+ keeps checking. Black is trying to move the king away from the c-file’s critical entry squares.
Kb4 steps down while keeping c5 covered. Promoting does not yet permit a safe rook skewer.
Rd4+ follows the king down the board.
Kb3 keeps c4 controlled. Each retreat preserves the same geometric protection one rank lower.
Rd3+ checks again. White has reached a point where the edge of the board changes the rook’s possibilities.
Kc2 escapes the checks while controlling b1, b2 and c1. A skewer from below is no longer available.
Rd4 sets a different trap: a queen promotion permits ...Rc4+ and stalemate after the rook is captured.
c8=R avoids the queen’s stalemate trap. After ...Rc4+ and Rxc4, the escape square a2 remains available.
Ra4 meets the immediate Ra8 mate threat along the a-file.
Kb3 attacks the rook on a4 and renews the mating threat. The king makes the two rooks unequal.
Rc4+ is an illustrated last check. White can capture because the king on b3 protects c4.
Rxc4 leaves a winning rook-versus-king ending. Black’s king still has a legal move, so the game continues instead of ending in stalemate.
branches.explanation: Rxc4 leaves a winning rook-versus-king ending. Black’s king still has a legal move, so the game continues instead of ending in stalemate.

branches.title: Try keeping the king near promotion
commentary: Staying close to the pawn looks natural. Check whether that closeness lets the rook pin it.
Kb7 puts king and pawn on the seventh rank. White’s winning chance is gone with best defense.
Rd7 pins c7 against the king on b7. White cannot simply push the pawn and force a winning promotion; the tablebase result is a draw.
branches.explanation: Rd7 pins c7 against the king on b7. White cannot simply push the pawn and force a winning promotion; the tablebase result is a draw.

branches.title: Promote to a queen and test the trap
commentary: The strongest piece is not always the winning promotion. Check what happens if Black can sacrifice the rook with tempo.
c8=Q allows Black to use the queen’s long diagonals to remove the last king escape.
Rc4+ checks and attacks the queen on c8. White must resolve the check; taking the rook looks like the cleanest answer.
Qxc4 is stalemate. The king on c2 covers b1 and b2, and the queen on c4 covers a2 along c4-b3-a2. Black’s king on a1 has no move.
branches.explanation: Qxc4 is stalemate. The king on c2 covers b1 and b2, and the queen on c4 covers a2 along c4-b3-a2. Black’s king on a1 has no move.

branches.title: Compare the same trap against a rook
commentary: Use the same defensive idea to see precisely what the underpromotion changes.
c8=R promotes without giving the new piece a queen’s diagonal control.
Rc4+ is still legal, but its stalemate trick has disappeared.
Rxc4 captures the rook. The king on c2 covers b1 and b2, but the rook on c4 does not control a2. Black still has a legal king move.
Ka2 is legal, so there is no stalemate. White retains the standard winning rook-versus-king ending.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Ka2 is legal, so there is no stalemate. White retains the standard winning rook-versus-king ending.

exercises.prompt: Why does Kb5 work better than Kb7?
exercises.answer: Kb7 permits a rook pin on d7. Kb5 instead covers c6, stopping the rook from establishing a safe skewer after promotion.

exercises.prompt: Which legal king move distinguishes rook promotion from queen promotion?
exercises.answer: After c8=R Rc4+ Rxc4, the rook does not control a2. Black can play Ka2, so it is not stalemate. The queen on c4 would control a2.

verification_scope: Selected positions reconstructed from saved source images. Every encoded move and intermediate outcome is checked; representative replies illustrate the idea without enumerating every legal defense.
